Cooling Tower Drift Eliminators: Types, Functions & Maintenance

  • Tim Bozic
  • July 3, 2026
  • 9:56 am

Table of Contents

Cooling towers are intricate systems with numerous engineered parts working together, but few are as critical to environmental compliance and water conservation as drift eliminators. These often-overlooked components play a key role in reducing water loss and ensuring regulatory standards are met.

Neglecting them during routine maintenance can lead to decreased efficiency, higher operational costs, and potential compliance issues. By prioritizing drift eliminators, you not only enhance your cooling tower’s performance but also contribute to sustainable water usage and long-term savings.

Failure to manage drift can lead to significant water waste, chemical carryover, and damage to nearby infrastructure. In this guide, we’ll explore how they work, the different types available, the key performance metrics to look for, and the critical factors to keep in mind when choosing the right one for your facility.

What Are Drift Eliminators in Cooling Towers?

Basic Function and Purpose

They are specialized baffles designed to capture water droplets entrained in the cooling tower air stream. While evaporation is a necessary part of the heat rejection process, “drift” refers to liquid water droplets that are mechanically carried out of the tower by the exhaust air.

These droplets contain dissolved solids, treatment chemicals, and bacteria present in the circulating water. Drift eliminators are strategically installed at the air discharge section of the tower to separate these droplets from the air stream.

The primary functions of these components include:

  • Minimizing Water Loss: They prevent valuable process water from escaping into the atmosphere.
  • Preventing Nuisance: They stop water from settling on nearby buildings, cars, and equipment.
  • Environmental Protection: They reduce the emission of chemicals and particulate matter.

Why Drift Eliminators Are Critical to Cooling Tower Performance

Water Conservation and Operating Cost Control

Uncontrolled drift represents a continuous loss of water volume that must be replaced. In large industrial cooling towers operating continuously, even a small percentage of drift loss translates to millions of gallons of wasted water annually.

They significantly reduce the requirement for makeup water. By keeping the circulating water within the system, facilities lower their water utility bills and reduce the volume of treatment chemicals required to maintain water quality.

Chemical Containment and Emissions Reduction

Water droplets escaping the tower carry the same chemical composition as the basin water. This includes corrosion inhibitors, biocides, and antiscalants. If these chemicals exit the tower as drift, they pose environmental and safety risks.

They act as a barrier, providing several key benefits:

  • Equipment Protection: They protect nearby electrical equipment from corrosion caused by chemical-laden water droplets.
  • Safety: They prevent ice from forming on adjacent structures during winter operations.
  • Regulatory Compliance: They help facilities comply with strict environmental regulations by reducing particulate emissions.

Impact on Overall Tower Efficiency

While the primary role of drift eliminators is water retention, they also influence the thermal performance of the tower. A well-designed eliminator stabilizes the airflow as it exits the fill media, ensuring uniform air distribution.

However, if they become clogged or are poorly designed, they create excessive resistance. This resistance restricts airflow, forcing fans to work harder and reducing the overall heat rejection capability of the cooling tower.

Types of Drift Eliminators Used in Industrial Cooling Towers

PVC Drift Eliminators

Polyvinyl Chloride (PVC) is the standard material for drift eliminators in most commercial and industrial applications. It offers a balance of durability and affordability, making it suitable for general water cooling duties.

PVC eliminators are typically UV-protected and resistant to rot, bacteria, and most water treatment chemicals. They are lightweight and easy to handle during installation and maintenance.

Key characteristics include:

  • Temperature Range: Suitable for standard operating temperatures up to approximately 120°F (49°C).
  • Chemical Resistance: Excellent resistance to acids, alkalis, and salts.
  • Cost: Generally, the most cost-effective option for standard applications.

FRP Eliminators

Fiberglass Reinforced Plastic (FRP) eliminators are engineered for more demanding environments. Facilities that process high-temperature water or deal with aggressive chemical concentrations often require the superior durability of FRP.

These units provide exceptional structural rigidity, allowing them to span longer distances without sagging. This structural integrity ensures consistent performance over a longer service life compared to standard plastics.

Key advantages include:

  • High-Temperature Tolerance: Capable of withstanding temperatures exceeding 120°F.
  • Structural Strength: High load-bearing capacity and impact resistance.
  • Corrosion Resistance: Superior protection against a wide range of industrial solvents and chemicals.

Cellular vs Blade-Type Designs

They generally fall into two structural categories: cellular (honeycomb) and blade-type. Cellular eliminators create a highly efficient, integrated structure that forces air through narrow, convoluted passages. Blade-type eliminators consist of individual slats arranged in a specific configuration.

Choosing between them often depends on the specific pressure drop requirements and maintenance capabilities of the facility.

Selection considerations include:

  • Cellular Designs: Offer high efficiency and low pressure drop, but are difficult to clean if fouled.
  • Blade-Type Designs: Allow for easier cleaning and inspection, but may require more complex installation hardware.
  • Application: Cellular types are common in modern package towers; blade types are often found in field-erected units.

Common Drift Eliminator Problems and Failure Modes

Fouling and Blockage

They are prone to accumulating debris over time. As the final stage before air exits, they can trap biological growth, scale, and airborne dust.

This fouling reduces the open area available for airflow. The consequences include increased fan energy usage, reduced cooling capacity, and uneven air distribution across the tower.

Common causes include:

  • Algae Growth: Sunlight exposure promotes biological activity.
  • Scale Formation: High mineral content in the water settles on the eliminator surfaces.
  • Process Contamination: Oil or grease in the water can stick to the blades.

Material Degradation

Harsh operating environments take a toll on drift eliminator materials. Constant exposure to UV radiation, temperature fluctuations, and chemical oxidizers eventually weakens the plastic or fiberglass structure.

Degradation often manifests as:

  • Brittleness: Materials crack or shatter under minor impact.
  • Warping: Thermal stress causes blades to deform, opening gaps for drift to escape.
  • Surface Erosion: Chemical attack roughens the surface, altering aerodynamic performance.

Improper Installation or Fitment

Even the highest quality drift eliminator will fail if installed incorrectly. Gaps between modules or between the eliminators and the tower casing create bypass paths.

Air follows the path of least resistance. If gaps exist, air will accelerate through them, carrying water droplets directly out of the tower and bypassing the eliminator media entirely.

Installation issues often include:

  • Poor Sealing: Lack of proper sealants or gaskets at the casing interface.
  • Sagging Supports: Inadequate structural support causes modules to separate.
  • Damaged Modules: Rough handling during installation creates breaks in the media.

Drift Eliminator Inspection and Maintenance Best Practices

Inspection Frequency and Access Points

Regular visual inspections are necessary to identify issues before they impact compliance or efficiency. Operators should inspect them at least annually, or more frequently in harsh environments.

Inspections should verify:

  • Cleanliness: Check for signs of scale or algae blockage.
  • Placement: Ensure all modules are seated correctly with no visible gaps.
  • Structural Integrity: Look for sagging supports or damaged blades.

Cleaning Methods That Do Not Damage Media

Cleaning it requires care to avoid damaging the relatively fragile fins or cellular structure. High-pressure washing is generally discouraged as it can shred PVC or dislodge modules.

Recommended cleaning approaches include:

  • Low-Pressure Rinse: Use a water spray to remove loose debris.
  • Chemical Cleaning: Apply foam cleaners to dissolve scale or biological growth, followed by a rinse.
  • Removal: For heavy fouling, remove modules to clean them on the ground to prevent debris from falling into the basin.

When Replacement Is Necessary

Cleaning can extend the life of drift eliminators, but eventually, replacement becomes the only viable option. Continuing to operate with degraded eliminators risks permit violations and equipment damage.

Indicators for replacement include:

  • Permanent Deformation: Warped modules that no longer fit together tightly.
  • Severe Brittleness: Material that cracks when touched or cleaned.
  • Persistent Drift: Visible water droplets exiting the tower despite cleaning.

Comparison Table – Drift Eliminator Types and Performance

How to Choose the Right Drift Eliminator for Your Cooling Tower

Operating Environment

The chemical and thermal conditions of your cooling water dictate the material selection. Standard commercial towers may function well with PVC, while industrial processes often require robust solutions.

Consider the following environmental factors:

  • Water Temperature: Does the application involve process upsets with high heat?
  • Water Chemistry: Are there high concentrations of solvents, oils, or acids?
  • UV Exposure: Is the discharge area subjected to intense direct sunlight?

Cooling Tower Type and Airflow Design

The physical configuration of the tower determines the shape and airflow characteristics required. You must match the eliminator design to the specific crossflow or counterflow arrangement of your equipment.

Technical specifications to review include:

  • Air Velocity: Ensure the eliminator is rated for the specific fan speed and airflow of the tower.
  • Pressure Drop: Verify the fan motor has sufficient power to overcome the resistance of the new eliminators.
  • Support Spans: Check if existing supports can handle the weight and span of the proposed modules.

Conclusion

Drift eliminators might seem like simple components, but they are carefully designed to protect your cooling tower’s performance. They play a crucial role in preventing water loss, chemical emissions, and potential damage.

Choosing the right eliminator involves factors such as material compatibility with your water chemistry and the design type that suits your tower’s airflow, like blade, cellular, or cross-fluted. It’s also important to consider environmental conditions such as water temperature and UV exposure, along with technical specifications like air velocity and pressure drop. Understanding these factors ensures your system operates efficiently and remains clean.

Ready to optimize your cooling tower’s performance? ICS offers a wide selection of high-quality drift eliminators designed for reliability and compliance. Explore our solutions today and invest in the long-term health of your equipment.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a drift eliminator in a cooling tower?

A drift eliminator is a component that captures water droplets from exhaust air to prevent water loss, chemical carryover, and environmental contamination.

Why are drift eliminators important in cooling towers?

They reduce water loss, control chemical emissions, protect nearby equipment, and help meet environmental compliance standards.

How much drift loss is acceptable in cooling towers?

Modern high-efficiency drift eliminators typically limit drift loss to 0.0005%–0.001% of circulating water flow.

What happens if drift eliminators fail or are damaged?

Failure can cause excessive water loss, chemical drift, corrosion of nearby structures, higher operating costs, and regulatory violations.

What are the main types of cooling tower drift eliminators? 

The most common types are PVC drift eliminators, FRP drift eliminators, and cellular or blade-type designs.

structures.text: Cooling towers are intricate systems with numerous engineered parts working together, but few are as critical to environmental compliance and water conservation as drift eliminators. These often-overlooked components play a key role in reducing water loss and ensuring regulatory standards are met.
structures.html: Cooling towers are intricate systems with numerous engineered parts working together, but few are as critical to environmental compliance and water conservation as drift eliminators. These often-overlooked components play a key role in reducing water loss and ensuring regulatory standards are met.

structures.text: Neglecting them during routine maintenance can lead to decreased efficiency, higher operational costs, and potential compliance issues. By prioritizing drift eliminators, you not only enhance your cooling tower’s performance but also contribute to sustainable water usage and long-term savings.

structures.text: Failure to manage drift can lead to significant water waste, chemical carryover, and damage to nearby infrastructure. In this guide, we’ll explore how they work, the different types available, the key performance metrics to look for, and the critical factors to keep in mind when choosing the right one for your facility.

structures.section: What Are Drift Eliminators in Cooling Towers?
structures.text: What Are Drift Eliminators in Cooling Towers?
structures.html: What Are Drift Eliminators in Cooling Towers?

structures.text: Basic Function and Purpose
structures.html: Basic Function and Purpose

structures.text: They are specialized baffles designed to capture water droplets entrained in the cooling tower air stream. While evaporation is a necessary part of the heat rejection process, “drift” refers to liquid water droplets that are mechanically carried out of the tower by the exhaust air.
structures.html: They are specialized baffles designed to capture water droplets entrained in the cooling tower air stream. While evaporation is a necessary part of the heat rejection process, “drift” refers to liquid water droplets that are mechanically carried out of the tower by the exhaust air.

structures.text: These droplets contain dissolved solids, treatment chemicals, and bacteria present in the circulating water. Drift eliminators are strategically installed at the air discharge section of the tower to separate these droplets from the air stream.
structures.html: These droplets contain dissolved solids, treatment chemicals, and bacteria present in the circulating water. Drift eliminators are strategically installed at the air discharge section of the tower to separate these droplets from the air stream.

structures.text: The primary functions of these components include:
structures.html: The primary functions of these components include:

structures.text: Minimizing Water Loss: They prevent valuable process water from escaping into the atmosphere. Preventing Nuisance: They stop water from settling on nearby buildings, cars, and equipment. Environmental Protection: They reduce the emission of chemicals and particulate matter.
structures.html:
• Minimizing Water Loss: They prevent valuable process water from escaping into the atmosphere.
  • Preventing Nuisance: They stop water from settling on nearby buildings, cars, and equipment.
  • Environmental Protection: They reduce the emission of chemicals and particulate matter.

structures.section: Why Drift Eliminators Are Critical to Cooling Tower Performance
structures.text: Why Drift Eliminators Are Critical to Cooling Tower Performance

structures.section: Water Conservation and Operating Cost Control
structures.text: Water Conservation and Operating Cost Control
structures.html: Water Conservation and Operating Cost Control

structures.section: Water Conservation and Operating Cost Control
structures.text: Uncontrolled drift represents a continuous loss of water volume that must be replaced. In large industrial cooling towers operating continuously, even a small percentage of drift loss translates to millions of gallons of wasted water annually.
structures.html: Uncontrolled drift represents a continuous loss of water volume that must be replaced. In large industrial cooling towers operating continuously, even a small percentage of drift loss translates to millions of gallons of wasted water annually.

structures.section: Water Conservation and Operating Cost Control
structures.text: They significantly reduce the requirement for makeup water. By keeping the circulating water within the system, facilities lower their water utility bills and reduce the volume of treatment chemicals required to maintain water quality.
structures.html: They significantly reduce the requirement for makeup water. By keeping the circulating water within the system, facilities lower their water utility bills and reduce the volume of treatment chemicals required to maintain water quality.

structures.text: Chemical Containment and Emissions Reduction
structures.html: Chemical Containment and Emissions Reduction

structures.text: Water droplets escaping the tower carry the same chemical composition as the basin water. This includes corrosion inhibitors, biocides, and antiscalants. If these chemicals exit the tower as drift, they pose environmental and safety risks.
structures.html: Water droplets escaping the tower carry the same chemical composition as the basin water. This includes corrosion inhibitors, biocides, and antiscalants. If these chemicals exit the tower as drift, they pose environmental and safety risks.

structures.text: They act as a barrier, providing several key benefits:
structures.html: They act as a barrier, providing several key benefits:

structures.text: Equipment Protection: They protect nearby electrical equipment from corrosion caused by chemical-laden water droplets. Safety: They prevent ice from forming on adjacent structures during winter operations. Regulatory Compliance: They help facilities comply with strict environmental regulations by reducing particulate emissions.
structures.html:
• Equipment Protection: They protect nearby electrical equipment from corrosion caused by chemical-laden water droplets.
  • Safety: They prevent ice from forming on adjacent structures during winter operations.
  • Regulatory Compliance: They help facilities comply with strict environmental regulations by reducing particulate emissions.

structures.text: Impact on Overall Tower Efficiency
structures.html: Impact on Overall Tower Efficiency

structures.text: While the primary role of drift eliminators is water retention, they also influence the thermal performance of the tower. A well-designed eliminator stabilizes the airflow as it exits the fill media, ensuring uniform air distribution.
structures.html: While the primary role of drift eliminators is water retention, they also influence the thermal performance of the tower. A well-designed eliminator stabilizes the airflow as it exits the fill media, ensuring uniform air distribution.

structures.text: However, if they become clogged or are poorly designed, they create excessive resistance. This resistance restricts airflow, forcing fans to work harder and reducing the overall heat rejection capability of the cooling tower.

structures.section: Types of Drift Eliminators Used in Industrial Cooling Towers

structures.text: PVC Drift Eliminators
structures.html: PVC Drift Eliminators

structures.text: Polyvinyl Chloride (PVC) is the standard material for drift eliminators in most commercial and industrial applications. It offers a balance of durability and affordability, making it suitable for general water cooling duties.
structures.html: Polyvinyl Chloride (PVC) is the standard material for drift eliminators in most commercial and industrial applications. It offers a balance of durability and affordability, making it suitable for general water cooling duties.

structures.text: PVC eliminators are typically UV-protected and resistant to rot, bacteria, and most water treatment chemicals. They are lightweight and easy to handle during installation and maintenance.
structures.html: PVC eliminators are typically UV-protected and resistant to rot, bacteria, and most water treatment chemicals. They are lightweight and easy to handle during installation and maintenance.

structures.text: Key characteristics include:
structures.html: Key characteristics include:

structures.text: Temperature Range: Suitable for standard operating temperatures up to approximately 120°F (49°C). Chemical Resistance: Excellent resistance to acids, alkalis, and salts. Cost: Generally, the most cost-effective option for standard applications.
structures.html:
• Temperature Range: Suitable for standard operating temperatures up to approximately 120°F (49°C).
  • Chemical Resistance: Excellent resistance to acids, alkalis, and salts.
  • Cost: Generally, the most cost-effective option for standard applications.

structures.text: FRP Eliminators
structures.html: FRP Eliminators

structures.text: Fiberglass Reinforced Plastic (FRP) eliminators are engineered for more demanding environments. Facilities that process high-temperature water or deal with aggressive chemical concentrations often require the superior durability of FRP.
structures.html: Fiberglass Reinforced Plastic (FRP) eliminators are engineered for more demanding environments. Facilities that process high-temperature water or deal with aggressive chemical concentrations often require the superior durability of FRP.

structures.text: These units provide exceptional structural rigidity, allowing them to span longer distances without sagging. This structural integrity ensures consistent performance over a longer service life compared to standard plastics.
structures.html: These units provide exceptional structural rigidity, allowing them to span longer distances without sagging. This structural integrity ensures consistent performance over a longer service life compared to standard plastics.

structures.text: Key advantages include:
structures.html: Key advantages include:

structures.text: High-Temperature Tolerance: Capable of withstanding temperatures exceeding 120°F. Structural Strength: High load-bearing capacity and impact resistance. Corrosion Resistance: Superior protection against a wide range of industrial solvents and chemicals.
structures.html:
• High-Temperature Tolerance: Capable of withstanding temperatures exceeding 120°F.
  • Structural Strength: High load-bearing capacity and impact resistance.
  • Corrosion Resistance: Superior protection against a wide range of industrial solvents and chemicals.

structures.text: Cellular vs Blade-Type Designs
structures.html: Cellular vs Blade-Type Designs

structures.text: They generally fall into two structural categories: cellular (honeycomb) and blade-type. Cellular eliminators create a highly efficient, integrated structure that forces air through narrow, convoluted passages. Blade-type eliminators consist of individual slats arranged in a specific configuration.
structures.html: They generally fall into two structural categories: cellular (honeycomb) and blade-type. Cellular eliminators create a highly efficient, integrated structure that forces air through narrow, convoluted passages. Blade-type eliminators consist of individual slats arranged in a specific configuration.

structures.text: Choosing between them often depends on the specific pressure drop requirements and maintenance capabilities of the facility.
structures.html: Choosing between them often depends on the specific pressure drop requirements and maintenance capabilities of the facility.

structures.text: Selection considerations include:
structures.html: Selection considerations include:

structures.text: Cellular Designs: Offer high efficiency and low pressure drop, but are difficult to clean if fouled. Blade-Type Designs: Allow for easier cleaning and inspection, but may require more complex installation hardware. Application: Cellular types are common in modern package towers; blade types are often found in field-erected units.
structures.html:
• Cellular Designs: Offer high efficiency and low pressure drop, but are difficult to clean if fouled.
  • Blade-Type Designs: Allow for easier cleaning and inspection, but may require more complex installation hardware.
  • Application: Cellular types are common in modern package towers; blade types are often found in field-erected units.

structures.section: Common Drift Eliminator Problems and Failure Modes
structures.text: Common Drift Eliminator Problems and Failure Modes
structures.html: Common Drift Eliminator Problems and Failure Modes

structures.section: Common Drift Eliminator Problems and Failure Modes

structures.text: Fouling and Blockage
structures.html: Fouling and Blockage

structures.text: They are prone to accumulating debris over time. As the final stage before air exits, they can trap biological growth, scale, and airborne dust.
structures.html: They are prone to accumulating debris over time. As the final stage before air exits, they can trap biological growth, scale, and airborne dust.

structures.text: This fouling reduces the open area available for airflow. The consequences include increased fan energy usage, reduced cooling capacity, and uneven air distribution across the tower.
structures.html: This fouling reduces the open area available for airflow. The consequences include increased fan energy usage, reduced cooling capacity, and uneven air distribution across the tower.

structures.text: Common causes include:
structures.html: Common causes include:

structures.text: Algae Growth: Sunlight exposure promotes biological activity. Scale Formation: High mineral content in the water settles on the eliminator surfaces. Process Contamination: Oil or grease in the water can stick to the blades.
structures.html:
• Algae Growth: Sunlight exposure promotes biological activity.
  • Scale Formation: High mineral content in the water settles on the eliminator surfaces.
  • Process Contamination: Oil or grease in the water can stick to the blades.

structures.text: Material Degradation
structures.html: Material Degradation

structures.text: Harsh operating environments take a toll on drift eliminator materials. Constant exposure to UV radiation, temperature fluctuations, and chemical oxidizers eventually weakens the plastic or fiberglass structure.
structures.html: Harsh operating environments take a toll on drift eliminator materials. Constant exposure to UV radiation, temperature fluctuations, and chemical oxidizers eventually weakens the plastic or fiberglass structure.

structures.text: Degradation often manifests as:
structures.html: Degradation often manifests as:

structures.text: Brittleness: Materials crack or shatter under minor impact. Warping: Thermal stress causes blades to deform, opening gaps for drift to escape. Surface Erosion: Chemical attack roughens the surface, altering aerodynamic performance.
structures.html:
• Brittleness: Materials crack or shatter under minor impact.
  • Warping: Thermal stress causes blades to deform, opening gaps for drift to escape.
  • Surface Erosion: Chemical attack roughens the surface, altering aerodynamic performance.

structures.text: Improper Installation or Fitment
structures.html: Improper Installation or Fitment

structures.text: Even the highest quality drift eliminator will fail if installed incorrectly. Gaps between modules or between the eliminators and the tower casing create bypass paths.
structures.html: Even the highest quality drift eliminator will fail if installed incorrectly. Gaps between modules or between the eliminators and the tower casing create bypass paths.

structures.text: Air follows the path of least resistance. If gaps exist, air will accelerate through them, carrying water droplets directly out of the tower and bypassing the eliminator media entirely.
structures.html: Air follows the path of least resistance. If gaps exist, air will accelerate through them, carrying water droplets directly out of the tower and bypassing the eliminator media entirely.

structures.text: Installation issues often include:
structures.html: Installation issues often include:

structures.text: Regular visual inspections are necessary to identify issues before they impact compliance or efficiency. Operators should inspect them at least annually, or more frequently in harsh environments.

structures.text: Inspections should verify:
structures.html: Inspections should verify:

structures.text: Cleanliness: Check for signs of scale or algae blockage. Placement: Ensure all modules are seated correctly with no visible gaps. Structural Integrity: Look for sagging supports or damaged blades.

  • Placement: Ensure all modules are seated correctly with no visible gaps.

structures.section: Cleaning Methods That Do Not Damage Media
structures.text: Cleaning it requires care to avoid damaging the relatively fragile fins or cellular structure. High-pressure washing is generally discouraged as it can shred PVC or dislodge modules.
structures.html: Cleaning it requires care to avoid damaging the relatively fragile fins or cellular structure. High-pressure washing is generally discouraged as it can shred PVC or dislodge modules.

structures.section: Cleaning Methods That Do Not Damage Media
structures.text: Recommended cleaning approaches include:
structures.html: Recommended cleaning approaches include:

structures.section: Cleaning Methods That Do Not Damage Media
structures.text: Low-Pressure Rinse: Use a water spray to remove loose debris. Chemical Cleaning: Apply foam cleaners to dissolve scale or biological growth, followed by a rinse. Removal: For heavy fouling, remove modules to clean them on the ground to prevent debris from falling into the basin.
structures.html:
• Low-Pressure Rinse: Use a water spray to remove loose debris.
  • Chemical Cleaning: Apply foam cleaners to dissolve scale or biological growth, followed by a rinse.
  • Removal: For heavy fouling, remove modules to clean them on the ground to prevent debris from falling into the basin.

structures.text: When Replacement Is Necessary
structures.html: When Replacement Is Necessary

structures.text: Cleaning can extend the life of drift eliminators, but eventually, replacement becomes the only viable option. Continuing to operate with degraded eliminators risks permit violations and equipment damage.
structures.html: Cleaning can extend the life of drift eliminators, but eventually, replacement becomes the only viable option. Continuing to operate with degraded eliminators risks permit violations and equipment damage.

structures.text: Indicators for replacement include:
structures.html: Indicators for replacement include:

structures.text: Permanent Deformation: Warped modules that no longer fit together tightly. Severe Brittleness: Material that cracks when touched or cleaned. Persistent Drift: Visible water droplets exiting the tower despite cleaning.
structures.html:
• Permanent Deformation: Warped modules that no longer fit together tightly.
  • Severe Brittleness: Material that cracks when touched or cleaned.
  • Persistent Drift: Visible water droplets exiting the tower despite cleaning.

structures.text: Operating Environment
structures.html: Operating Environment

structures.text: The chemical and thermal conditions of your cooling water dictate the material selection. Standard commercial towers may function well with PVC, while industrial processes often require robust solutions.
structures.html: The chemical and thermal conditions of your cooling water dictate the material selection. Standard commercial towers may function well with PVC, while industrial processes often require robust solutions.

structures.text: Consider the following environmental factors:
structures.html: Consider the following environmental factors:

structures.text: Water Temperature: Does the application involve process upsets with high heat? Water Chemistry: Are there high concentrations of solvents, oils, or acids? UV Exposure: Is the discharge area subjected to intense direct sunlight?
structures.html:
• Water Temperature: Does the application involve process upsets with high heat?
  • Water Chemistry: Are there high concentrations of solvents, oils, or acids?
  • UV Exposure: Is the discharge area subjected to intense direct sunlight?

structures.text: The physical configuration of the tower determines the shape and airflow characteristics required. You must match the eliminator design to the specific crossflow or counterflow arrangement of your equipment.

structures.text: Air Velocity: Ensure the eliminator is rated for the specific fan speed and airflow of the tower. Pressure Drop: Verify the fan motor has sufficient power to overcome the resistance of the new eliminators. Support Spans: Check if existing supports can handle the weight and span of the proposed modules.

  • Support Spans: Check if existing supports can handle the weight and span of the proposed modules.

structures.text: Conclusion
structures.html: Conclusion

structures.text: Drift eliminators might seem like simple components, but they are carefully designed to protect your cooling tower’s performance. They play a crucial role in preventing water loss, chemical emissions, and potential damage.
structures.html: Drift eliminators might seem like simple components, but they are carefully designed to protect your cooling tower’s performance. They play a crucial role in preventing water loss, chemical emissions, and potential damage.

structures.text: Choosing the right eliminator involves factors such as material compatibility with your water chemistry and the design type that suits your tower’s airflow, like blade, cellular, or cross-fluted. It’s also important to consider environmental conditions such as water temperature and UV exposure, along with technical specifications like air velocity and pressure drop. Understanding these factors ensures your system operates efficiently and remains clean.

structures.text: Frequently Asked Questions
structures.html: Frequently Asked Questions

structures.text: What is a drift eliminator in a cooling tower?
structures.html: What is a drift eliminator in a cooling tower?

structures.text: A drift eliminator is a component that captures water droplets from exhaust air to prevent water loss, chemical carryover, and environmental contamination.
structures.html: A drift eliminator is a component that captures water droplets from exhaust air to prevent water loss, chemical carryover, and environmental contamination.

structures.text: Why are drift eliminators important in cooling towers?
structures.html: Why are drift eliminators important in cooling towers?

structures.text: They reduce water loss, control chemical emissions, protect nearby equipment, and help meet environmental compliance standards.
structures.html: They reduce water loss, control chemical emissions, protect nearby equipment, and help meet environmental compliance standards.

structures.text: How much drift loss is acceptable in cooling towers?
structures.html: How much drift loss is acceptable in cooling towers?

structures.text: Modern high-efficiency drift eliminators typically limit drift loss to 0.0005%–0.001% of circulating water flow.
structures.html: Modern high-efficiency drift eliminators typically limit drift loss to 0.0005%–0.001% of circulating water flow.

structures.text: What happens if drift eliminators fail or are damaged?
structures.html: What happens if drift eliminators fail or are damaged?

structures.text: Failure can cause excessive water loss, chemical drift, corrosion of nearby structures, higher operating costs, and regulatory violations.
structures.html: Failure can cause excessive water loss, chemical drift, corrosion of nearby structures, higher operating costs, and regulatory violations.

structures.text: What are the main types of cooling tower drift eliminators?
structures.html: What are the main types of cooling tower drift eliminators?

structures.text: The most common types are PVC drift eliminators, FRP drift eliminators, and cellular or blade-type designs.
structures.html: The most common types are PVC drift eliminators, FRP drift eliminators, and cellular or blade-type designs.
